title: Empirical Evaluation of a Deterministic-Validator Guard for LLM→NetOps Generate→Verify→Repair Pipelines (Revised)
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment that measures the operational impact of inserting a deterministic network-configuration validator into an LLM-driven generate→verify→repair (GVR) loop for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a reproducible synthetic 200-task multi-vendor intent bank and a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) under an adapter contract (≤1 automated repair call per task), each task produced one shared initial candidate; the guarded artifact was the final configuration after deterministic validation and, if invoked, a single automated repair. Primary estimand: paired absolute difference in actionable-misconfiguration rate (guarded − baseline), implemented as paired success-rate difference per the preregistration. Results (N=200 pairs): baseline valid-config count = 199/200 (0.995), guarded valid-config count = 200/200 (1.000); absolute paired change (guarded − baseline) = 0.005 (0.5 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided test p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.015] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The preregistered primary hypothesis (≥50% relative reduction in actionable misconfigurations under original power assumptions) is not supported because the observed baseline error prevalence (1/200) was far lower than assumed in the preregistered power calculation. We reconcile estimand algebra, expand execution/accounting and reproducibility details, and point auditors to archived artifact paths and SHA-256 digests for forensic verification.

sections.introduction: Motivation and question. Converting operator intent into device-specific configuration via generative LLMs promises efficiency gains in Network Operations (NetOps) but raises safety concerns: incorrect or out-of-order commands can violate workflow policies or cause outages. Practitioners commonly propose inserting deterministic validators and automated repair loops into generate→verify→repair (GVR) pipelines as operational guardrails. Yet rigorous, preregistered, artifact-hashed quantification of the marginal operational benefit from such validators under bounded adapter contracts is scarce. We preregistered study cnsmspec2026_gvr_v1_prereg_001 (SHA-256 = 5cb8a30815eacf0a3ca659d1a54fbaa71218e5ce57c0b13e2658099eb7da6ee4) to answer: How much does integrating a deterministic network validator into an LLM-driven GVR pipeline reduce actionable misconfiguration rates (paired comparison) on a 200-task synthetic multi-vendor NetOps task bank, and what residual error types persist after automated repairs? Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (success = not actionable error). Key contribution: a fully preregistered, artifact-hashed, paired confirmatory run with deterministic validator traces and complete provider-call accounting for forensic auditors.
sections.related_work: Deterministic network verification and runtime validators (e.g., header-space analysis [1], VeriFlow [2]) are standard pre-deployment safety mechanisms. Recent LLM→NetOps studies (e.g., NetConfEval [3], Lira et al. [4]) evaluate intent→config generation accuracy but rarely measure the incremental operational effect of an intervening deterministic validator under a frozen initial candidate and a bounded repair budget. Our experiment differs in four practical ways: (1) shared_initial generation: the LLM produces one candidate reused across baseline and guarded conditions, eliminating confounding from generation variance; (2) deterministic validator: per-episode canonical ASTs, vendor-aware parsing, and simulator-backed semantic checks; (3) adapter contract: at most one automated repair call per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1); (4) forensic archival: cryptographic SHA-256 digests for preregistration, raw results, model configuration, and per-episode scoring JSONs so auditors can deterministically reconstruct contingency tables and validator traces.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The preregistration froze the paired binary design (N=200 tasks, planned strata: Cisco-like 66; Juniper-like 67; RFC-neutral 67), the primary estimand (paired absolute difference in success rate), the confirmatory test (exact two-sided McNemar), and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The registry also defined missingness, retry, and exclusion rules and an explicit multiplicity plan (single primary hypothesis H1; secondary/exploratory tests labeled accordingly).

Adapter, model, and generation semantics. Execution used adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and requested_model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA-256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The adapter enforced shared_initial generation (independent_condition_generation = false) so the same LLM candidate was scored under both baseline and guarded paths. The adapter contract permitted at most one repair call per task; provider-call accounting (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA-256 = 8a2b85f8...) records hosted_model_call_event_count = 201 with stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation:200, repair:1}, matching model_calls_used = 201 in execution manifest (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA-256 = 9eeaa0c8...). These authoritative hashes are archived.

Synthetic task bank and deterministic validator. Tasks were generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and encode initial_state, expected_final_state, workflow policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields), permitted touched fields, and required_sequence. The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) performs: (a) vendor-aware parse into canonical AST; (b) syntactic and vendor-constraint checks; (c) intent-constraint verification against required_sequence and workflow policies; and (d) simulator-backed semantic checks capturing multi-step dependencies. The validator emits per-episode validator_trace objects (validation_before, validation_after) and a binary score using scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation. Representative per-episode scoring JSONs and their SHA-256 digests are archived under execution/scoring/ (example: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json SHA-256 = 079a6390d5...).

Execution, retries, and missingness. The preregistered retry policy allowed up to two automatic retries on provider-call failures before exclusion; no provider-call failures occurred. Execution manifest: planned_episode_count = 400 (200 pairs × 2), completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, complete_pair_count = 200 (execution manifest SHA-256s recorded). Missingness_summary.csv (analysis/missingness_summary.csv SHA-256 = 808b3c00...) shows complete_pairs = 200 with zero exclusions. All provider calls, retries (none), and stage counts are logged and hashed for reproducibility.

Statistical analysis. The analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 consumed execution/raw_results.jsonl and produced the paired contingency counts n_11,n_10,n_01,n_00, the exact McNemar two-sided p-value, and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute paired difference (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). The analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA-256 = 658051ba..., analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA-256 = 86ab6b56...) are archived and authoritative.
sections.results:
Primary outcome (artifact-grounded). Complete_pair_count = 200; baseline_success_count = 199 (0.995); guarded_success_count = 200 (1.000); absolute paired change (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. Contingency counts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA-256 = 658051bae1f10d90aed1728b8d20dd3700a5694b68b02f1b0c118c45d9414db0): n_11 = 199 (guarded=1 & baseline=1), n_10 = 1 (guarded=1 & baseline=0; guarded-only improvement), n_01 = 0 (guarded=0 & baseline=1), n_00 = 0 (both invalid). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI for absolute paired difference = [0.0, 0.015] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729).

Interpretation of the confirmatory result. The preregistered H1 targeted a ≥50% relative reduction in actionable-error rate. Algebraic mapping: actionable_error_rate = 1 − success_rate. Observed baseline actionable-error rate = 1 − 0.995 = 0.005 (1/200). A 50% relative reduction corresponds to an absolute reduction of 0.0025 (from 0.005 → 0.0025). The absolute effect we observed (0.005 → 0.0) equals 0.005 in absolute units and reduces the baseline actionable-error rate to zero; however, the preregistered power calculation had assumed a much larger baseline error prevalence and was sized to detect absolute differences on the order of ≈0.15. Given the extremely small discordant-pair mass (n_10 + n_01 = 1), the exact McNemar test yields p = 1.0 and the paired bootstrap CI includes zero; under the preregistered confirmatory decision rule we therefore cannot claim statistical support for the preregistered large-effect hypothesis. This is a design–realization mismatch: the guarded pipeline achieved a numerically favorable outcome but the original power calibration was not appropriate for a rare-failure operating regime.

Representative forensic trace. The single discordant improvement (n_10 = 1) is present as an explicit per-episode record in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA-256 = 9eeaa0c8...) and in the per-episode scoring JSONs under execution/scoring/; auditors can retrieve the full validator_trace, provider-call trace, and raw LLM response using the archived manifests (execution/execution_manifest.json lists all file paths and full hash manifest). To preserve forensic determinism we provide the authoritative artifact pointers and SHA-256 digests (Disclosure Statement) rather than reproduce full per-episode traces inline here.
sections.discussion:
Operational implications. In workflows where an LLM baseline already produces extremely few actionable errors (here 1/200), the marginal absolute benefit of a deterministic validator + single automated repair may be numerically small even if the relative reduction is large. System designers should align validation and repair investment with expected baseline error prevalence and risk costs: (1) if baseline errors are common, validators+repairs can deliver large absolute risk reduction; (2) if baseline errors are rare, designers should consider targeted validation on high-difficulty subsets, increased N for evaluation, or cost-weighted estimands that reflect outage costs rather than raw proportions.

Design lessons and post-hoc sensitivity. The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute change much larger than observed. A post-hoc sensitivity observation using archived counts and the bootstrap CI ([0.0,0.015]) shows that while the observed absolute improvement point estimate is small (0.005), the CI upper bound (0.015) is still far below the preregistered absolute MDE ≈0.15 assumed in design. Thus the study is underpowered for the originally targeted absolute effect in the realized rare-failure regime. Practical corrective options for future runs (artifact-grounded): increase N, oversample high-difficulty tasks where baseline error mass concentrates (task generator difficulty fields are archived per task), or use a cost-weighted estimand sensitive to rare high-cost failures (task manifests encode per-task required_sequence and difficulty metadata useful for such weighting).

Threats to validity. Internal: prompt sensitivity and single-model evidence (gpt-5-mini) limit internal robustness. Construct: synthetic task bank and deterministic validator semantics bound real-world representativeness. External: single-model, single-validator, and bounded repair-budget limit generalizability. Conclusion validity: rare-event regime yields low discordant mass and wide relative uncertainty for small absolute effects. We enumerate these limitations and provide artifact-grounded mitigation suggestions in the reproducibility notes below.

Reproducibility and forensic artifacts. Key archived, authoritative digests: preregistration SHA-256 = 5cb8a30815eacf0a3ca659d1a54fbaa71218e5ce57c0b13e2658099eb7da6ee4; model_configuration.json SHA-256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820; execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA-256 = 9eeaa0c87db4742c807240b5ee18f934aaf45848350b3840f92af401bcb68d02; execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA-256 = 4b28215e8a611feda50f6284058083b9ffcc2f5881f557081ce9e9f890f1c78a; deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA-256 = 8a2b85f8260409eebce1641421af6a74f1c479e505bdef805314510e25931891; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA-256 = 658051bae1f10d90aed1728b8d20dd3700a5694b68b02f1b0c118c45d9414db0; analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA-256 = 86ab6b56e3ec10aa54aa08480a8e1ef31b64d79bf22bc99dac1d8ed00628a68a. These artifacts provide deterministic reconstruction of every reported count, CI, and per-episode trace.

Reviewer requests and archival policy. Reviewers requested (i) explicit per-vendor stratified observed counts and (ii) the explicit discordant episode identifier. The preregistration contains the planned stratum sizes (Cisco-like 66; Juniper-like 67; RFC-neutral 67). Observed per-vendor stratified results are fully computable from execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA-256 = 4b28215e8a611feda50f6284058083b9ffcc2f5881f557081ce9e9f890f1c78a) and per-episode scoring JSONs under execution/scoring/ (full file list and hashes in execution/execution_manifest.json). Because those exact observed per-vendor numeric summaries and the explicit discordant episode id are not printed verbatim in the supplied manuscript evidence bundle, we provide authoritative artifact pointers and SHA-256 digests here so auditors can deterministically extract and verify the numbers and full traces. This avoids introducing unverifiable inline numerics while preserving forensic reproducibility. If reviewers specifically request the inline numeric table and episode id, we will include them verbatim in a subsequent revision only after extracting them deterministically from the archived JSONs and recording their derived-hash provenance in the manuscript.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment evaluating the marginal effect of inserting a deterministic validator into an LLM→NetOps GVR pipeline under a bounded adapter contract. On a synthetic 200-task bank with gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5, guarded success increased from 199/200 to 200/200 (absolute paired change = 0.005). The preregistered large-effect hypothesis (sized for much larger absolute differences) is not supported because the observed baseline error prevalence (1/200) was far lower than assumed in power planning. We publish cryptographic digests and precise artifact paths for all principal inputs, provider calls, validator traces, and analysis outputs to enable deterministic audit and extension. Future work should broaden model and validator diversity, increase repair budgets, and adapt estimands to rare high-cost failure regimes.

limitations: Single-model evidence: only gpt-5-mini was used; results do not imply multi-model generality.
Synthetic task bank and validator scope: the 200-task benchmark and deterministic validator semantics bound external validity to production networks.
Low baseline error prevalence: baseline actionable-error rate = 1/200, limiting power to detect moderate relative improvements and making effect-size estimates imprecise for rare failure regimes.
Single automated repair attempt: the adapter contract permitted at most one automated repair per task; multi-attempt repair effects are unexplored.
Single deterministic validator implementation: validator coverage or implementation choices influence measured outcomes; different validators may yield different paired results.

Untestable preregistered secondary hypothesis (H2): because guarded residual failures = 0, the preregistered confirmatory contingency test comparing residual error-type proportions could not be executed and any error-type comments are exploratory.

Reviewer-required per-vendor stratified observed counts and explicit discordant episode identifier are not included verbatim in the supplied manuscript evidence bundle; auditors can compute them from execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA-256 = 4b28215e8a611feda50f6284058083b9ffcc2f5881f557081ce9e9f890f1c78a) and execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA-256 = 9eeaa0c87db4742c807240b5ee18f934aaf45848350b3840f92af401bcb68d02) but we do not invent those numeric summaries or identifiers in the manuscript where they are not present verbatim in the supplied archive.
